latin.363: §. II. Consubstantiatio, quae, vi etymi, duarum Substantiarum, per se sejunctarum Conjunctionem, vel in actu, vel in statu considerandam, significat, alia Crassior est, alia Subtilior. Prior corporis Christi naturalis & localis, vel in pane inclusionem localem, vel unionem interiorem commixtioni physicae, seu miscibilium alteratorum elementorum unioni haud absimilem, denotat.
latin.364: Hanc, utroque modo conceptam, à Luthero, post rejectam ab eo Transsubstantiationem, edoctam contendunt ejus Adversarii. Carlstadius, priorem modum Luthero impingit, ipsummet ita allocutus: Du wirst mich lang nicht überreden daß GOtt im Brod sey? Item: Wie kan man Christum ins Brod und Wein bringen?
latin.365: Posteriorem, Unionem scil. corporis Christi cum pane personalem, eoque intimam & perichoristicam, Lutherum inculcasse in duobus sensibus, prolixius exponit Becanus, Manual. Controv. lib. 2. cap. 2. quest. 2. p. 330. Et sanè vero Lutherus utriusque modi à se asserti, formulis suis loquendi, haud levem suspicionem genuerit, quando ex una parte, verba Christi, hoc est corpus meum, tùm in prosa oratione, per tres has particulas, In, Cum, & Sub hoc pane est corpus meum, tum in ligata Cantione à se composita: JEsus Christus unser Heyland &c. / per hunc rythmum, verborgen im Brod so klein / gab Er uns seinen Leib zu essen / explanavit, hancque suam Explanationem Impanationis & Companationis titulis gravandi ansam dedit amplissimam.
latin.366: Ex altera parte, Unionem panis & Corporis Christi in Eucharistia cum Unione humanae Christi naturae, & personae ejus divinae, in libro de Captivitate Babylonica Tom. 2. mihi p. 265. eum in modum comparat, ut huic per omnia similem fecisse visus sit; tamen, quia tum ipse Lutherus posteriorem Unionis modum, seu personalem, conceptis verbis in Confessione sua majore de Coena, negat; in Libro autem de Captivitate Babylonica, Transsubstantiationem pontificiam refutaturus, panisque in Coena praesentiam adstructurus, inter propositiones has duas: Hoc, seu, hic panis est corpus meum, Et, Deus est homo, nudam duntaxat earum comparationem instituisse deprehenditur & ostendere gestivisse, quô modô utrobique Disparatum de Disparato praedicetur; (Quô nomine etiam inter nostrates Wolfgangus Musculus, Lutherum à personali corporis & sanguinis Christi Unione absolvit Loci commun. p. m. 354.)
latin.367: Tùm verò formulis loquendi, priorem Unionis modum invehentibus, nil aliud sibi voluisse à Lutheranis perhibetur, quàm inexplicabilem Coëxistentiae corporis Christi cum pane rationem, denotare, eandem ob causam nunquam unâ vel alterâ ex tribus particulis, In, Cum, & Sub, separatim acceptâ, sed universis simul sumtis, usus (cujus tamen contrarium vidimus Annot. praeced. §. 3. 4.); Nec non in rythmo, solam Imperceptibilitatem modi praesentiae corporis Christi in Eucharistia, vocabulo germanico hoc, Verborgen / exprimere sat egisse, hunc in sensum rythmo integro exponendo: JEsus gab uns in dem so kleinen Brod / seinen Leib / verborgen / das ist / auf verborgene unbegreifliche und geheime Weise / zu essen; idcirco (utut expositiones ac excusationes Lutheri ejusque formularum loquendi, satis violente contortaque maneant) non tamen vel Luthero ipsi, quantum ad hactenus ab eo dicta attinet, vel Lutheranis hodiernis, Crassiorem istam Consubstantiationem rectè tribui posse arbitramur.
latin.368: Posterior, seu Subtilis Consubstantiatio, solam dicit duarum Substantiarum, panis scil. & Corporis Christi in S. Coena Coëxistentiam Unionemque quandam exteriorem, ac παραστατικήν, dicendam equidem Substantialem, Corporalem, Localem, at non Formaliter, seu quoad Unionis modum, sed solum Materialiter & quoad ipsa Unienda, quae omnino Substantiae & quidem Corporeae sunt, indeque porrò suum quaelibet locum proprium, localitatemque intrinsecam, obtinent. Hujus Definitionem, seu essentiales conceptus jamjam nominatos, cùm Lutherani nulli dubitaverint suos facere, etiam Definitum sive latino Consubstantiationis, sive graeco συνουσίας termino expressum, facilè admiserint, uti colligere datur ex Kronmayeri Theol. Posit. p. 703. & 714. & Bayeri Dissert. de Impanatione p. 31. quanquam ab admisso Definito hoc, nulla Synusiastas eos appellandi justa procedat consequentia, nec diffitendum sit, si genuinum & patristicum συνουσίας & συνουσιαστῶν usum sequaris, Lutheranos non συνουσιάστας, sed ἐνουσιάστας rectius appellari, sic merito monente Suicero, Thesaur. Eccles. p. 1183. & 1184.; Justius verò Becanus cit. a pag. 331. inferat, datâ Consubstantiatione quacunque, etiam Lutherana tantum, & subtiliori, propriae praedicationi verborum Christi locum ampliùs nullum relinqui.

pass_a.363: §. II. Consubstantiation, which by force of etymology signifies the Conjunction of two Substances severed in themselves, to be considered either in act or in state, is partly Crasser, partly Subtler. The former denotes either a local inclusion of Christ’s natural and local body in the bread, or an interior union not unlike a physical mixture, or the union of altered miscible elements.
pass_a.364: His Adversaries contend that Luther, after he rejected Transubstantiation, taught this [crasser mode] conceived either way. Carlstadt charges the former mode on Luther, addressing him thus: You will not long persuade me that God is in the bread? Likewise: How can one bring Christ into bread and wine?
pass_a.365: Becanus (Manual of Controversies bk. 2 ch. 2 q. 2 p. 330) expounds at length that Luther inculcated the latter — namely a personal, and so intimate and perichoretic, Union of Christ’s body with the bread — in two senses. And truly Luther by his own formulas of speech generated no light suspicion of either mode asserted by him, when on the one hand he explained Christ’s words This is my body both in prose by these three particles In, With, and Under this bread is my body, and in a bound Song composed by himself — Jesus Christ our Savior &c. — by this rhythm, hidden in the bread so small / He gave us His body to eat — and gave amplest occasion for loading that Explanation with the titles Impanation and Companation.
pass_a.366: On the other hand, in On the Babylonian Captivity Tom. 2 at my p. 265 he compares the Union of bread and Christ’s Body in the Eucharist with the Union of Christ’s human nature and His divine person in such a way that he seems to have made it altogether like that; yet because Luther himself denies the latter, personal, mode of Union in express words in his Greater Confession on the Supper; and in On the Babylonian Captivity, about to refute pontifical Transubstantiation and build the bread’s presence in the Supper, he is found to have instituted only a bare comparison between these two propositions — This, or this bread is my body, and God is man — and to have wished to show how in both a Disparate is predicated of a Disparate; (on which account among our people also Wolfgang Musculus absolves Luther from a personal Union of Christ’s body and blood, Common Places p. m. 354.)
pass_a.367: But as for formulas of speech that seem to bring in the former mode of Union, the Lutherans maintain he meant nothing other than to denote the inexplicable reason of the Coexistence of Christ’s body with the bread — and for the same cause never used one or another of the three particles In, With, and Under taken separately, but all taken together (of which nonetheless we saw the contrary in the preceding Annotation §§.3–4); and that in the rhythm he was content enough to express only the Imperceptibility of the mode of presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist by this German word Verborgen / hidden — explaining the whole rhythm in this sense: Jesus gave us in the so small bread / His body / hidden / that is / in a hidden, incomprehensible and secret way / to eat; therefore (however violently twisted Luther’s expositions and excuses of his formulas of speech remain) we judge that that Crasser Consubstantiation cannot rightly be attributed either to Luther himself, so far as what he has said hitherto, or to today’s Lutherans.
pass_a.368: The latter, or Subtle Consubstantiation, says only a Coexistence of two Substances — namely bread and Christ’s Body in the Sacred Supper — and a certain exterior and parastatic Union, to be called indeed Substantial, Corporal, Local, yet not Formally, or as to the mode of Union, but only Materially and as to the things to be united, which are altogether Substances and indeed Corporeal, and thence each obtains its own proper place and intrinsic locality. Since no Lutherans have hesitated to make this Definition, or the essential concepts just named, their own, they have also easily admitted the Defined expressed either by the Latin term of Consubstantiation or by the Greek συνουσία — as may be gathered from Kronmayer’s Positive Theology pp. 703 and 714 and Bayer’s Dissertation on Impanation p. 31 — although from this admitted Defined no just consequence proceeds of calling them Synusiasts, nor is it to be denied that if you follow the genuine and patristic use of συνουσία and συνουσιασταί, Lutherans are more rightly called ἐνουσιάσται, not συνουσιάσται, Suicer rightly warning so (Thesaurus Ecclesiasticus pp. 1183–1184); but more justly Becanus (cited from p. 331) infers that given any Consubstantiation whatsoever — even only the Lutheran and subtler — no place is left any longer for the proper predication of Christ’s words.

363: §.II: Consubstantiation, by etymology, is the joining of two substances kept apart in themselves — considered in act or in state.
It comes in a crasser and a subtler form. The crasser means either local enclosure of Christ’s natural body in the bread, or an interior union like a physical mixture of altered elements.
364: Adversaries say Luther taught that crasser mode after he rejected Transubstantiation.
Carlstadt pins local enclosure on him: You will not long persuade me that God is in the bread — and How can one bring Christ into bread and wine?
365: Becanus (Manual Controv. II.2.2 p. 330) charges Luther with a personal, intimate, perichoretic union of body with bread.

Luther’s own speech feeds the suspicion: In, With, and Under this bread is my body, plus his hymn line hidden in the bread so small / He gave us His body to eat — ample handle for Impanation and Companation labels.
366: In On the Babylonian Captivity he compares bread–body union with the hypostatic union (Deus est homo), which looks personal.

Yet his Greater Confession on the Supper denies a personal mode, and the Captivity comparison is only bare Disparate-of-Disparate predication — so Musculus (among ours) absolves him from personal union of body and blood.
367: Lutherans say the crasser-sounding formulas only mark inexplicable coexistence — hence In/Cum/Sub used together, never apart (though Annotatio I §§.3–4 showed the contrary).
Verborgen in the hymn means only that the mode of presence is imperceptible — hidden, incomprehensible, secret.
However forced the excuses, Strimesius will not rightly pin that crasser Consubstantiation on Luther or today’s Lutherans.
368: Subtler Consubstantiation: bread and Christ’s body coexist in the Supper with an exterior, παραστατική union — substantial/corporal/local materially as to the things united, not formally as to union-mode; each keeps its own place.
Lutherans own the definition and the name Consubstantiation / συνουσία (Kronmayer; Bayer) — yet Suicer would call them ἐνουσιάσται, not συνουσιάσται.
Becanus’s sharper point: grant any Consubstantiation, even the Lutheran subtler kind, and proper predication of Christ’s words has nowhere left to stand.
